summary:
Trans visitors face a severe and divided risk environment. Two separate criminal-law regimes apply across the Palestinian territories, and the difference between them is decisive: consensual same-sex conduct is not an offence in the West Bank, while in Gaza the same conduct is punishable by up to ten years' imprisonment under a statute that has been enforced against LGBT people.

The West Bank operates under the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960. Jordan's 1951 revision of its own code dropped offences against consensual private sexual conduct and the 1960 code carried that position forward, so no provision criminalises consensual same-sex acts there. The Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality, and Israel stopped applying the older Mandate criminal code in 1977.

Gaza is governed by Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936, which remains in force. Section 152(2) punishes consensual same-sex 'carnal knowledge' with up to ten years' imprisonment, and the same code sets out broader historic terms, including sodomy with up to fourteen years and an 'act against the law of nature' with up to ten years. Section 152(1)(c), the only youth-linked provision cited, carries up to fourteen years for sodomy with a child under sixteen. The Human Rights Watch and the Human Dignity Trust hold the 1936 ordinance to be in force in Gaza; its applicability is contested by other commentators, and Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal there.

No provision of either regime expressly prohibits trans identity, but the 1936 code's public-morality provisions are broad enough to catch trans people in practice. No legal gender recognition provisions are set out for the territories, and Equaldex reports no broad legal protections against discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people.

Formal legality does not describe what is encountered on the ground. Social and family persecution makes daily reality harsher than the written law, and periodic transphobic threats and attacks are recorded. Palestinian police action against a planned event organised by al-Qaws drew a wave of hate messages that activists said posed a serious threat to the community, and rights groups condemned the police ban on LGBTQ activity. Palestinian Authority non-signatory status to key human rights treaties limits the protection machinery available to a visitor.

HIV prevention and care are inadequate. HIV-positive queer individuals often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and stigma is high, and epidemiological surveillance is lacking: only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered between 1988 and 2017, with the true figure believed to be far higher because taboos hinder data collection. In Gaza since October 2023, the collapse of the healthcare system together with Israeli blockades has made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult.

Entry runs through Israel. Around 90 LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence, and since June 2022 Israel has issued work permits to gay Palestinians granted asylum and to those fleeing domestic violence. LGBTQ Palestinian asylum seekers in Israel are routinely excluded from basic healthcare programmes and shelter access available to other asylum seekers, and some have faced house arrest or deportation.
tangentialFactors:
The legal picture is a patchwork of Ottoman, British, Jordanian, Egyptian and Israeli layers rather than a single code, so a visitor's exposure depends on which territory and which authority is present. Applicability of the 1936 ordinance is genuinely disputed: the Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force in Gaza, Amnesty does not report same-sex acts as illegal, and the legal commentator Anis F. Kassim has argued it could be read as permitting homosexuality.

A 2003 draft Palestinian penal code would have criminalised adult consensual same-sex conduct, with up to five years for male-male sodomy; whether it was ever implemented is unknown, and the Palestinian Authority has not enacted a replacement.

Public attitudes are unfavourable and static. Palestine ranks 130 on a global social-acceptance index, with very little change between 2010 and 2020, and civil society groups protecting women and children are described as vulnerable to attack in Gaza.

Islamist actors contest LGBTQ content in education and youth spaces. The Palestinian Mujahideen Movement and the Rightly-Guided Caliphs Assembly criticised UNRWA for promoting what they regard as un-Islamic values including LGBTQ issues, and the Islamic Movement in Israel opposed Israel's conversion therapy ban; activist Maisan Hamdan has noted that the movement's stated aim is Palestine's liberation without LGBTQ inclusion.

Regional context cuts both ways. Human Rights Watch documented in 2018 that LGBT people across the Middle East and North Africa are building cross-border alliances and national and regional movements combating homophobia and transphobia, but Cairo 52's assessment of the occupation is that it marginalises queer and trans Palestinians alongside the wider population, documenting de facto oppression rather than formal protection.
localsOnly:
Residents live under a legal order the Palestinian Authority has not amended: it has passed no statute for or against homosexuality, and no legal gender recognition procedure exists. The practical pressure comes from family and community rather than prosecution, and queer Palestinians reported widespread discrimination and abuse in public and family settings in interviews conducted by the Women's Centre for Legal Aid and Counselling with Equality Now.

Statelessness is cited as a structural condition of LGBTQ Palestinians, and Palestinian queer organisations operate from within Israel rather than from the territories. The 2003 draft penal code remains on record as a legislative proposal that would have criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, so residents face the possibility of a future statutory change as well as present social enforcement.

Only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered between 1988 and 2017, comprising 79 AIDS cases and 19 HIV-positive diagnoses, and continuous antiretroviral therapy is frequently interrupted. Comprehensive epidemiological surveillance is lacking, and Gaza's healthcare collapse since October 2023 has hit HIV medication supply hardest.

Israeli policy toward residents who flee is conditional. Around 90 LGBT Palestinians have been granted temporary asylum permits, work permits began to be issued only in June 2022 for those granted asylum or fleeing domestic violence, and asylum seekers are excluded from basic healthcare and shelter provision, with some facing house arrest or deportation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The in-force status of the 1936 British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance in Gaza is unresolved in the sources: the Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force, Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal there, and Anis F. Kassim has argued it could be read as permitting homosexuality. This record follows the Human Rights Watch and Human Dignity Trust position while noting the disagreement.

Whether the 2003 draft Palestinian penal code was implemented is not established in any source consulted.

The gap between officially registered HIV cases and actual prevalence is acknowledged but not quantified; the true number is described only as likely far higher.

Incident-level documentation of transphobic violence in the territories is thin: sources record periodic threats and attacks without dated case details or outcomes, and no named trans-specific killing or prosecution in either territory was located in this inventory.

No source consulted sets out an entry, visa or border-screening rule that turns on gender marker or trans status for visitors arriving via Israel or via the Jordanian and Egyptian crossings.
